## Left open by the earlier read (RD-013)

An independent reader judged the previous rewrite of this lesson. Fix everything below as well. Each item is as serious as an item under "Fix these".

### Findings

1. Rule L18 (Major). Problem: The worked ground-classification cases cover bribery, culpable constitutional violation, and betrayal of public trust, but the brief also asks for meaning/application of treason, graft and corruption, and other high crimes. Those distinct ground applications have no worked example.
   > An impeachable officer is accused of accepting money in exchange for an official act. Which named impeachment ground most directly fits the accusation?
extra_brief.lesson-philippine-constitution-bill-of-r:
## Left open by the earlier read (RD-013)

An independent reader judged the previous rewrite of this lesson. Fix everything below as well. Each item is as serious as an item under "Fix these".

### Findings

1. Rule L18 (Major). Problem: This worked case covers court access, but the brief separately requires legal assistance despite poverty and the lesson has no worked case where legal assistance is denied for that reason. The custodial examples also do not directly test the right to remain silent as a distinct application.
   > A person is told that a court will not accept the case only because the person is poor. Which protection applies?
2. Rule L25 (Major). Problem: The lesson introduces the legal term "compelled self-incrimination" without explaining its meaning before the learner needs it to understand the confession rule. No prerequisite lesson is supplied in the packet.
   > A confession or admission obtained in violation of Section $12$, or of the right against compelled self-incrimination in Section $17$, cannot be used as evidence against the person.

## Left open by the earlier read (RD-013)

An independent reader judged the previous rewrite of this lesson. Fix everything below as well. Each item is as serious as an item under "Fix these".

### Findings

1. Rule L18 (Major). Problem: The worked human-rights case asks for the first analysis step and later mentions a remedy, but the brief separately requires explaining effects of human-rights violations. No worked example asks the learner to identify or explain those effects.
   > A detainee says officers used degrading physical punishment. What should be checked first when analyzing the claim?
2. Rule L26 (Major). Problem: The phrase "the kind of result protected by law" is left undefined, so the general double-jeopardy rule is not taught well enough for a learner to know when the first case creates the protection. The later worked case covers only the special law-and-ordinance situation.
   > **Double jeopardy** protects a person from being placed in jeopardy of punishment twice for the same offense after the first criminal case has reached the kind of result protected by law.
3. Rule L27 (Major). Problem: This states the special law-and-ordinance condition, but the lesson never states the relevant conditions for the general same-offense double-jeopardy protection. Without those limits, the learner cannot tell when the general rule applies.
   > The Constitution also gives a special rule when the same act is punished by both a law and an ordinance. A conviction or acquittal under either one bars another prosecution for the same act under the other.
